steps.title: The world's funniest joke, allegedly
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 147 words

A group of researchers who called themselves LaughLab spent a year collecting jokes from the public and asking the internet to rate them. They received over forty thousand, and they did find differences between countries.

Several European countries, among them France, Denmark and Belgium, preferred jokes about subjects that usually make people anxious: illness, death, the things nobody wants to discuss. If you joke about it, one researcher suggested, it frightens you slightly less.

English-speaking countries preferred wordplay. Germany, unless the results were badly skewed, liked almost everything equally, which the press reported as proof that Germans have no sense of humour and which, if anything, suggests the opposite.

The joke that won was about two hunters, one of whom collapses. Provided that you have not heard it, it is quite good. Almost nobody who reads about the study ever laughs at it.

steps.title: Why a joke does not survive the border
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 148 words

A joke works by setting up an expectation and then breaking it. The final line — the punchline — has to arrive at the moment you are most confident about where the sentence is going.

This is why jokes travel so badly. Unless the audience shares the expectation, there is nothing to break. A joke that is hilarious in one country can be merely pointless in another, not because the humour is different but because the set-up has not been built.

Timing does the same work. As long as the punchline arrives at the right moment it can be very ordinary and still land; if it arrives a second late, even a witty line becomes predictable.

The most reliable finding in the whole field is unglamorous. Provided that the audience does not see it coming, almost anything is funny; and once they do, nothing is.

steps.title: unless, as long as, provided that, in case, even if
steps.html:
Five conjunctions that all set a condition, and all mean something slightly different.

unless = if not. Unless the audience shares the expectation, there is nothing to break. Never make the verb negative as well: unless they don't share it means the opposite.

as long as and provided that both mean only on this condition. Provided that is more formal and slightly stricter; as long as is neutral. As long as the punchline arrives on time, it can be ordinary.

in case is not a condition at all. It gives a precaution: you do something because it might happen, not if it happens. I don't tell that joke in case somebody is offended = I don't tell it, at all, as a precaution. Compare I won't tell it if somebody is offended, which makes no sense as a plan.

even if concedes: Even if it arrives on time, the joke is weak. The condition does not change the outcome.

All of these take a present tense for a future meaning, exactly like if: unless it arrives on time, never unless it will arrive.

Punctuation: when the clause comes first, put a comma after it. When it comes second, no comma: Provided that you have not heard it, it is quite good / It is quite good provided that you have not heard it.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two texts.

If you joke about it, it frightens you slightly less.
Plain condition.

Germany, unless the results were badly skewed, liked everything equally.
Unless = if not.

Provided that you have not heard it, it is quite good.
Formal condition, clause first, comma after.

Unless the audience shares the expectation, there is nothing to break.
Positive verb after unless.

As long as the punchline arrives at the right moment, it can be ordinary.
Present for future.

If it arrives a second late, even a witty line becomes predictable.
Condition and consequence.

Provided that the audience does not see it coming, almost anything is funny.
The negative goes in the clause, not in provided.

I don't tell those jokes in case somebody is offended.
A precaution, not a condition.

Even if the timing is right, the joke is weak.
Concession.

It is quite good provided that you have not heard it.
Clause second, no comma.

Unless you don't tell me, I won't know.
Double negative — unless already means if not.

Unless it will arrive on time…
Present tense for future meaning.

steps.title: if / unless / in case, on the same facts
steps.html:
1. The situation: some people find a particular joke offensive, and you are deciding whether to tell it.
  2. If somebody is offended, I'll apologise. A condition: the apology happens only in that case.
  3. Unless somebody objects, I'll tell it. = if nobody objects. Note the positive verb after unless.
  4. I won't tell it in case somebody is offended. A precaution: you are not telling it at all, because the risk exists. This is the one learners most often get wrong.
  5. And the concession: Even if nobody objects, I still won't tell it. The condition is satisfied and the outcome does not change.

steps.title: You are going to review something you watched.

options.label: Something everybody else found funny and you did not
A performance of any kind you would recommend with conditions

steps.title: Write your review.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Rate it precisely, and attach at least three conditions to your recommendation using unless, as long as, provided that or even if.
steps.html:
• Open with a rating and one condition attached to it.
  • Describe the best part, using at least two precise adjectives.
  • Say where it goes wrong, using <i>as long as</i> or <i>once</i>.
  • Close with a recommendation and a concession using <i>even if</i>.

Useful language

  • It is genuinely witty, provided that you …
  • Unless you have seen … , the first twenty minutes will …
  • As long as you are not expecting … , it works.
  • Even if you dislike … , the last scene is worth it.
  • I would not watch it again in case it turns out to be …
  • Nothing in it is distasteful; it is simply …
steps.modelHtml:
Two hours I would mostly recommend

The first half is genuinely witty, provided that you can tolerate a slow opening. Almost nothing happens for twenty minutes, and unless you know that in advance you will assume you have chosen badly.

What follows is the best thing I have seen this year. The central performance is comical without ever becoming ridiculous, and there is one scene — a conversation across a table, in near silence — that is far more thought-provoking than the description suggests.

The last half hour is where it goes wrong. As long as the story stayed small it worked; once it tries to explain itself it becomes predictable, and the final line is the only tedious thing in it.

Watch it, then. Even if you dislike the ending, the middle hour is worth the whole evening.
